Deeper check of the instrument cluster
While parked, also reads the instrument cluster in its extended diagnostic session (looking for the odometer). Nothing is written; the cluster is put back in its normal session afterwards.

Type what the dashboard shows at the start and at the end of the drive, so the recording can be checked against it.
Tap the mode you switch the car to, so the recording knows how each stretch was driven.
Type the odometer and the range (distance to empty) from the dashboard when you set off, and again when you stop.
Enter the end odometer and range
The drive is over: type what the dashboard shows now, so the trip can be checked.
The end odometer is below the start (%1$s km). Check the number.
Tap Eco, City or Sport whenever you switch the car\'s mode.
Connect to the car first: the mode is written into the drive\'s recording.
Some of the car\'s units were not read yet. With the car parked and the engine on, you can run the check again; it only asks what is left.
Keep the car parked, %1$d s left
The car\'s speed still could not be read after about 10 seconds. Make sure the engine is on, then try again.
Passive capture only listens to what the car broadcasts and asks it nothing; live values pause meanwhile. Use it for a stretch of the drive, then go back.
No refuel seen yet. One is noticed when the fuel level jumps up, also after the car was switched off to fill it.
A new scan takes several minutes with the car parked and replaces the result shown now.
Android may pause KnightLink in the background to save battery, which stalls the sensors of the phone and can drop the adapter link while you drive. Allowing background running keeps it going.
Park the car with the ignition on, then start the scan. It reads everything the car answers, changes nothing, and takes about ten minutes. It pauses by itself if the car moves.
Scan: checking readiness and on-board tests on control unit %1$s, %2$d of %3$d.
Reading fault codes from control unit %1$s, %2$d of %3$d.
Scan paused: the car is moving at %1$d km/h. It goes on when you park.
Scan paused: the car is moving. It goes on when you park.

Scan finished. Minutes taken: %1$d. Control units found: %2$d. Fault codes, confirmed: %3$d, pending: %4$d, asking for the warning lamp: %5$d. Further codes that only say a test has not run, which are not faults: %6$d.
Scan stopped early: %2$s. What it found so far is kept. Minutes taken: %1$d. Control units found: %3$d.
Scan stopped by you. What it found so far is kept. Minutes taken: %1$d. Control units found: %2$d.
Scan interrupted: the connection to the adapter was lost. What it found so far is kept and the scan can be resumed. Minutes taken: %1$d. Control units found: %2$d.
KnightLink records the motion sensors of the phone with each drive, so the data of the car can be read next to how the car moved.
The location of the phone is recorded too. It stays on this phone; a shared copy has it rounded to about a kilometre.
Location is not recorded. Allow it to record where the drive was, for speed and bearing checks. It stays on this phone; a shared copy has it rounded to about a kilometre.
Not listening: Bluetooth is off, or the Nearby devices or precise Location permission is missing. Nothing is recorded.
Listening. Nothing heard yet: the sensors send about once a minute, and some only once the car moves. The Location setting of the phone must be on too.
Read with the sensor layouts (%1$s). Compare with the sensor app on the spot. No alerts.
No adapter found. Plug it into the car, make sure the ignition is on, and scan again.

KnightLink needs to find and connect to your OBD adapter over Bluetooth, and to hear your tyre sensors. Android calls this the Nearby devices permission, and also asks for Location, because tyre sensors send the same kind of signal as location beacons. Bluetooth scans are never used to work out where you are; your position is only recorded with a drive, and a shared copy has it rounded to about a kilometre.
The permission was blocked. Open the app settings, choose Permissions, and allow it there.
Adapter speed: about %1$s requests per second
%1$s: %2$s, stale, seconds since the last update: %3$d

Not available on this car means the app asked and the car did not offer it. That is a fact about the car, not a fault.
only on cars with a full profile
Used only to work out what a drive cost. It stays on your phone.
This makes one file. You choose where to send it; the app uploads nothing.

• The protocol, and the car's make, model and model year
• The manufacturer code from the VIN (its first three characters)
• The control units that answered, the data they support and their calibration ids
• Fault codes and emission readiness
• App and adapter versions, and a random id of this file
• A recording of the car's conversation with the adapter, with your phone's motion readings and the drive mode buttons you pressed
• The result of the full scan, if you ran one

• The VIN
• Your location: no GPS at all
• Your name
• The odometer and range you typed, and tyre sensor readings
• Clock times: times in the recording count from its start
